nodes.label: Deliberate Mixed-Bucket Under-Report
nodes.rationale: A foreign object whose stored length happens to be one a chain could have is reported short by the framing overhead; the alternative is a HeadObject per key, the round trip this design exists to avoid. Pinned by a test so nobody later fixes it with a per-key HEAD.

nodes.label: Item 1.2 Blanket 30s Read/Write Timeouts
nodes.rationale: ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout are wall-clock budgets for the entire body read or response write, not for a stalled one, so the effective object-size cap is 30s times client bandwidth. Replace with ReadHeaderTimeout plus per-copy-iteration deadlines via http.NewResponseController.

nodes.label: N-1 Fail-Open Pass-Through Read
nodes.rationale: GET/HEAD/ranged GET fell back to pass-through when an object carried no s3ep-* metadata even under an encrypting provider, so a backend stripping metadata had its substitute delivered as plaintext. Decided: fail closed, no opt-out knob.

nodes.label: N-5 Dead Rate-Limiting Knobs
nodes.rationale: Per-IP limiting is the wrong tool for an S3 proxy: any S3 client legitimately bursts from one address (Velero from one pod IP), and the failed-attempt map was keyed by an attacker-chosen X-Forwarded-For value and never expired.

nodes.label: BREAKING: metadata_key_prefix must match ^[a-z0-9-]+$
nodes.rationale: An empty value, previously documented in the README as a way to store metadata unprefixed, now refuses to start because it broke decryption.

nodes.norm_label: breaking: /debug/pprof on its own loopback listener
nodes.rationale: monitoring.pprof_enabled no longer serves /debug/pprof on monitoring.bind_address; pprof_bind_address must be a loopback address and is reached with an SSH tunnel or kubectl port-forward.

nodes.label: Breaking Change Guard
nodes.rationale: Version 4.0.0 was cut by accident on 2026-09-07: a coverage pull request was merged with a merge commit, two of its commits carried honest breaking markers and the release automation computed a major nobody had planned. A published tag cannot be withdrawn, so a breaking marker reaching main must be declared in advance rather than discovered afterwards.

nodes.label: Pull-request title and body inspection
nodes.rationale: Under a squash merge the title and body become the commit message the release analyser reads, so they carry breaking markers as much as the commits do. They are attacker-controlled text and are passed through the environment, never interpolated into the script, so shell metacharacters in a title cannot run on the runner. The merge base rather than the recorded base SHA is used so a pull request is not blamed for breaking commits it inherited.

nodes.label: npm clean-install --ignore-scripts under a write token
nodes.norm_label: npm clean-install --ignore-scripts under a write token
nodes.rationale: The job runs before review with a token that can push contents, so a dependency install script does not get to run with it; npm audit signatures then checks provenance attestations and registry signatures of what was installed.

nodes.label: Version Dry Run job
nodes.rationale: ADR 0018 D6: on every pull request into main the release tool computes the next version and prints it, so a major is merged against a number the tool produced rather than a human reading of the commits. Nothing is tagged, changed or released. Same-repository pull requests only, because semantic-release verifies push access with a git push --dry-run before analysing anything and a fork token is read-only.

nodes.label: Item 4a Refuse A Client Key Inside The Prefix
nodes.norm_label: item 4a refuse a client key inside the prefix
nodes.rationale: Both write paths drop such a key silently today; the work is 400 InvalidArgument naming the key, on every PUT and CreateMultipartUpload path.

nodes.label: Item 14 Metadata Prefix Shape
nodes.rationale: Pattern becomes ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{2,}-$: at least four characters, ending in a dash. What the rule still leaves open, reported rather than widened: no maximum length, and changing one valid prefix to another still passes startup while making every stored object unreadable - loudly now, InvalidObjectState on every read verb.

nodes.rationale: helm upgrade with a changed config updates the ConfigMap, reports success and leaves the old pods running the old configuration. An operator who rotates a KEK and is told it succeeded, while the old key still encrypts every new object, has been given a false statement about the security of their data by the deployment tooling.

nodes.label: Item 3 Probes Ignore tls.enabled
nodes.rationale: A plaintext httpGet against a TLS listener gets a 400 from Go's HTTP server, so the pod never becomes Ready with no hint why. The failure mode pushes operators towards running the proxy in plaintext, which is the wrong direction.

nodes.label: Item 6 Moving metadata_key_prefix Is Breaking
nodes.rationale: Moving the key under encryption: turns x-s3ep- from an ignored line into the live namespace, so every object an existing default install wrote under s3ep- reads back as a foreign object. Three ways out: move it and set the shipped default, delete the line, or accept the data becoming unreadable.

nodes.label: Demo Vault Defects
nodes.rationale: Unpinned image, the address exported after the wait loop so that loop may talk to the wrong address, obsolete login syntax, an rsa-2048 transit key nothing will use, and an empty mounted init directory.

nodes.label: Five Decisions Before Any Vault Code
nodes.norm_label: five decisions before any vault code
nodes.rationale: Library choice (a hand-rolled client reimplements TLS trust, retry semantics and token lifetime, where a subtle bug is a security bug); an optional key_scope fingerprint salt (without it the fingerprint on every object is a guessable hash of mount plus key name); explicit allow_plaintext_transport (a MITM on the Vault channel sees every data key in plaintext); the rewrap tool shipped with the provider; token-only authentication first.

nodes.label: Three Rotation Mechanisms
nodes.rationale: Scheduled rotation is free and rewrites nothing; retiring an old key version needs a rewrap campaign then a raised floor and rewrites the whole bucket; moving to a different key adds a second provider and switches the alias. They must never be confused. Routine rotation is only free because the key version is not part of the fingerprint - that is the design constraint everything hangs on.

nodes.label: Vault Transit As A KEK Provider
nodes.norm_label: vault transit as a kek provider
nodes.rationale: Talk to the Transit engine directly with a widely used library rather than completing the Tink stub, which would have existed solely as a wrapper around one HTTP call on a deprecated module path.

nodes.label: The DEK Cache Lifetime Becomes A Security Parameter
nodes.norm_label: the dek cache lifetime becomes a security parameter
nodes.rationale: With a network-backed provider the cache stops being an optimisation: it keeps repeat reads off the network, and a cached key keeps serving after Vault access is revoked. No value is right for both concerns. Today it is an LRU bounded at 1024 with no expiry at all; adding one is a prerequisite, not part of the work. There is also no request coalescing around the unwrap, so parallel ranged reads would burst identical Vault calls.

nodes.label: Key Custody Is What This Buys, And Only That
nodes.norm_label: key custody is what this buys, and only that
nodes.rationale: The key leaves the configuration file and the deployment secret. A compromised proxy still holds plaintext and can still ask Vault to unwrap anything it can present, for as long as its token is valid. Any sentence that blurs the two is a claim the product does not honour.

nodes.label: A Rewrap Campaign Is Not A Metadata Edit
nodes.norm_label: a rewrap campaign is not a metadata edit
nodes.rationale: Writing a rewrapped key back means a server-side copy that replaces metadata, and S3 rewrites the object to do that: a 5 TB campaign is a 5 TB rewrite even though no ciphertext byte changes. On a versioned or object-locked bucket it cannot retire a key version at all. It cannot run through the proxy - a copy primitive there would be a metadata-rewrite primitive for every authenticated client.

nodes.label: Vault Availability Becomes Proxy Availability
nodes.rationale: Cold reads fail during an outage and the proxy refuses to start without a reachable key, which during a rolling update turns an outage into a deployment that cannot scale back up. Correct and dangerous; it belongs in the operator documentation as the headline.

nodes.label: Verify First: Nothing Here Was Checkable
nodes.norm_label: verify first: nothing here was checkable
nodes.rationale: The design was written without network access, so every statement about the Vault API is from knowledge; the first task is an afternoon of curl against the demo Vault, capturing real request and response bodies into the file.

nodes.label: Start with the Graphify Knowledge Graph
nodes.norm_label: start with the graphify knowledge graph
nodes.rationale: The committed graph predates the 5.0.0 removal, so it is used for shape and never for facts until rebuilt; a graph hit is a pointer to verify in code, and rebuilding is a manual, user-approved step.

nodes.label: The Configuration Is a ConfigMap
nodes.rationale: A key written into config is readable by anyone with get configmaps in the namespace, which is why the chart ships no value for the master key; secrets in values files are base64, not encryption, and land in Helm's release history. The default config also reuses one key pair for the backend and for clients — a client holding the backend key reaches the bucket directly.

nodes.label: The Chart Has No Key for the Master Key
nodes.norm_label: the chart has no key for the master key

nodes.label: Decisions Live in ADRs
nodes.rationale: An ADR states what the product does and why and carries no references into the code (no paths, symbols or package names) so it stays true when the tree moves. It is written in the session the decision is taken, not when the work finishes.

nodes.label: A Ticket Is a Work List That Gets Deleted
nodes.norm_label: a ticket is a work list that gets deleted
nodes.rationale: A backlog that outlives its work costs focus. Nothing outside docs/tickets/ may reference a ticket; durable content moves to an ADR, README or SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE before the file is deleted.

nodes.label: Client-Driven Multipart Session Flow
nodes.rationale: The proxy owns the part layout it stores: the session's part table is the authority at Complete, not the list the client sends. A short part can only be a last part, so it is buffered; the inferred part size only ever takes a part that could be a middle part, because uploaders routinely deliver the short last part first.

nodes.label: The Honest Gap: One Forward Pass, No Tail-First Read
nodes.norm_label: the honest gap: one forward pass, no tail-first read
nodes.rationale: Status and Content-Length are already sent when the body starts flowing, so a fault found at the end cuts the body short at a segment boundary instead of answering an S3 error; x-amz-checksum-crc32c is served nowhere.

nodes.label: Exactly Four Metadata Keys
nodes.rationale: Only the prefixed key is ever read, because the unprefixed name lies outside the proxy's namespace and a client could set it through x-amz-meta-*. provider_alias is never stored.

nodes.label: PUT Request Data Flow
nodes.rationale: Every metadata value exists before the first backend byte, which is why no write path rewrites the finished object afterwards; the body seals as the backend pulls it so no write path materialises more than one segment.

nodes.label: 64 KiB-Multiple Part Rule
nodes.rationale: Every part but the last must cover whole 64 KiB segments and clear S3's 5 MiB minimum; the last part is held in memory until Complete so the trailer can follow it, bounded by multipart_short_part_buffer_size, and a client over that limit gets 503 SlowDown and retries.

nodes.label: Session Expiry Drops Proxy State, Not the Backend Upload
nodes.norm_label: session expiry drops proxy state, not the backend upload

nodes.label: Multipart Session Sweeper Leak, Fixed
nodes.rationale: The sweep walked the old, always-empty session map while the live map had a sweeper nothing called, so an abandoned upload held its data key and its buffered short part for the life of the process; Manager.Shutdown is now reached from the proxy's own shutdown so the goroutine cannot outlive it.

nodes.label: Where the Failure Surfaces
nodes.rationale: Two shapes: anything decided from metadata is an S3 error before the response begins; a fault found while streaming can only abort the body. A prefix of authentic plaintext — up to n-1 whole segments — is released first, and the abort is the only signal, so a client that treats ErrUnexpectedEOF as a transport flake accepts a truncated object as a complete one.

nodes.label: Values Nothing Reads
nodes.rationale: logging.*, serviceMonitor.port, secrets.gcp and secrets.aws change no rendered manifest; they are listed so nobody spends an afternoon on them, and the misplaced metadata_key_prefix under a provider config leaves the effective prefix at the default.

nodes.label: H-10 Three Configuration Decisions Specified and Not Built
nodes.norm_label: h-10 three configuration decisions specified and not built
nodes.rationale: One key that does half of what its name says, one bound (max_presign_expiry_seconds) the decision promises and the product does not offer, and no refusal to start on a plain-http backend under an encrypting provider.

nodes.label: H-5 A Tampered Object Is Delivered — closed
nodes.norm_label: h-5 a tampered object is delivered — closed
nodes.rationale: Measured across six attacks: each aborts the body and the prefix received is byte-identical to the object's own opening plaintext. The knob that appeared to control it is gone, because a build that skipped verification could not decrypt either.

nodes.label: H-7 Dead Security Configuration Knobs — closed
nodes.norm_label: h-7 dead security configuration knobs — closed
nodes.rationale: Six s3_security keys were parsed, defaulted, range-checked and documented and read by nothing. The one piece of machinery that looked like an implementation was worse than the absence it hid: it keyed a failure count on an attacker-chosen X-Forwarded-For value, compared it to a hardcoded 5, only logged, and never expired — so unauthenticated requests grew proxy memory without bound under a name that read like brute-force protection. Per-IP limiting was also the wrong tool: one authenticated client bursts from one address.

nodes.label: ListParts Still Pretends
nodes.rationale: It answers 200 with an always-empty result and never asks the backend, so a client cannot discover what an upload holds; the part table it could be answered from now exists on the session, and the handler does not read it.

nodes.label: Transport on Both Legs
nodes.rationale: The scheme in target_endpoint decides backend TLS; use_tls was deleted because it was read only to assign itself. Nothing refuses an http:// backend under an encrypting provider, and a listener on that leg learns every key name and object size even though the bytes stay sealed.

nodes.label: Integrity Is Not Configurable
nodes.rationale: Integrity is inseparable from decryption: the tag on each segment is produced by the same operation that encrypts it, so there is no off/lax/strict/hybrid mode to get wrong and no pass-through opt-out.

nodes.label: SSL_CERT_FILE Points at the Test CA
nodes.norm_label: ssl_cert_file points at the test ca
nodes.rationale: Go reads SSL_CERT_FILE for the system root pool, so the proxy validates the MinIO certificate for real instead of falling back to insecure_skip_verify. The backend endpoint is HTTPS because the SDK can only send an unseekable stream with UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and only over TLS.

nodes.norm_label: the backend is an adversary (d1, d2)

nodes.label: kopia Repository Password Must Be Set First
nodes.norm_label: kopia repository password must be set first
nodes.rationale: Velero writes velero-repo-credentials with the hardcoded static-passw0rd when the secret is missing, and an existing repository keeps the password it was created with, so this cannot be fixed afterwards; with the default, kopia's AES-GCM and content HMACs are forgeable by anyone who can read the bucket.

nodes.label: Pre-Signed URL Validation
nodes.rationale: X-Amz-Expires is mandatory and bounded to the AWS maximum of 7 days, and the signing time is subject to max_clock_skew_seconds so a URL cannot extend its own lifetime by claiming to have been signed in the future.

nodes.label: Ranged Reads
nodes.rationale: A range fetches only the segments its window covers and opens each under its own tag, so a partial read is authenticated like a whole one; Content-Range describes plaintext offsets so a client never has to know the object is stored encrypted. Suffix and open-ended ranges cost a HEAD because they are relative to the end; under the exit provider every range costs one, because that bucket holds both kinds of object.

nodes.label: Velero Deployment Notes
nodes.rationale: Point the BackupStorageLocation at the proxy over HTTPS with s3ForcePathStyle, because modern AWS SDKs only emit the checksum-trailer framing the proxy must decode over TLS; set publicUrl when the CLI runs outside the cluster.

nodes.label: The Clock-Skew Knob Governs Half of What Its Name Says
nodes.norm_label: the clock-skew knob governs half of what its name says
nodes.rationale: The header form uses the compile-time MaxClockSkewSeconds = 900 and ignores s3_security.max_clock_skew_seconds, which governs the pre-signed form only — so an operator who narrows the window narrows half of it.

nodes.label: H-1 Ranged Reads Are Not Verified — closed
nodes.norm_label: h-1 ranged reads are not verified — closed
nodes.rationale: What remains is inherent to any per-segment format: a range authenticates only the segments in its window, and one that does not reach the end never sees the trailer, so it trusts the backend's reported size. Pinned by a test so nobody 'fixes' it by reading more than was asked for.

nodes.label: H-4 Velero kopia Repositories Default to a Published Password
nodes.norm_label: h-4 velero kopia repositories default to a published password
nodes.rationale: Upstream, not a proxy defect: with the default password the repository salt sits in the same bucket, so kopia is neither confidentiality nor integrity against this backend — which leaves the proxy as the only protection for the resource tarballs Velero never encrypts at all.

nodes.label: SigV4 Validation, Header and Pre-Signed
nodes.rationale: Authentication failures return a fixed message per error code: the raw error text carried the attempted access key and header names, so reflecting it echoed attacker-controlled text into the body and broke the XML on & or <.

nodes.label: Client Checksums Are Neither Forwarded Nor Verified
nodes.norm_label: client checksums are neither forwarded nor verified
nodes.rationale: A client checksum describes the plaintext while the uploaded body is ciphertext, so a digest-checking backend would answer BadDigest for a good upload; responses carry no backend checksum for the mirror-image reason.

nodes.label: Bounded DEK LRU Cache
nodes.rationale: 1024 entries keyed by fingerprint, object key and a hash of the wrapped DEK, so a re-upload cannot serve a stale DEK; bounded with no expiry, which is a prerequisite for any provider with a network round trip behind it.

nodes.label: An Attacker Who Takes the Proxy Gets Everything
nodes.norm_label: an attacker who takes the proxy gets everything
nodes.rationale: KEK in process memory, the DEK cache, every in-flight plaintext, the backend credential and every client credential in plaintext. There is no key isolation, no HSM path and no separate signing identity that survives a proxy compromise.

nodes.label: What Is NOT Verified
nodes.rationale: The payload (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD is accepted, so the signature covers the request line and headers, not the bytes), per-chunk signatures, client checksums, replay within the 15-minute window, /health and /version, and the whole monitoring listener.

nodes.label: pprof on Its Own Loopback Listener
nodes.norm_label: pprof on its own loopback listener
nodes.rationale: A heap profile of this process contains DEKs and plaintext buffers, so a non-loopback pprof_bind_address is a startup error and the endpoint is not reachable on the published monitoring port; reach it from a container sharing the proxy network namespace.

nodes.label: H-2 Per-Chunk Signatures Are Never Verified
nodes.norm_label: h-2 per-chunk signatures are never verified
nodes.rationale: Accepted: chunk signatures protect the client leg while the adversary is on the other leg. The seed signature never covered the body, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD is already accepted, and verifying the chain costs real CPU where client checksum verification buys most of the same benefit.

nodes.label: pprof Must Bind Loopback or Startup Fails
nodes.norm_label: pprof must bind loopback or startup fails
nodes.rationale: /debug/pprof/heap on a process holding KEK material, DEKs and plaintext buffers is a key disclosure primitive; the previous log line telling the operator to restrict access was a control that existed only in documentation. Decoupling it from monitoring.enabled removed the same class of lie.

nodes.label: Three Write Paths, Identical Bytes
nodes.rationale: All three paths produce identical bytes, so nothing about a stored object says how it was uploaded.

nodes.label: The Backend Refuses an aws-chunked Chunk Above 16 MiB
nodes.norm_label: the backend refuses an aws-chunked chunk above 16 mib
nodes.rationale: A single PutObject of a large body makes the SDK emit one chunk the size of the body; the proxy accepts it because it decodes the framing and re-frames towards the backend, so the direct leg fails where the proxy leg succeeds and both legs switch to multipart above 16 MiB — a comparison between two different client methods is not a comparison.

nodes.label: Uniform Measurement Record Schema
nodes.rationale: Every measurement has the same shape whatever produced it, so two runs diff without per-instrument parsing; ratios are never stored so both legs stay visible and a missing leg shows as missing rather than as a plausible number. A run also records the machine, including power source, because two runs from different machines are not comparable.

nodes.label: How Big a Change Has to Be to Be Real
nodes.norm_label: how big a change has to be to be real
nodes.rationale: Identical code measured between 6.5% slower and 8.9% faster at 1 MiB and above, and swung 13% at 64 KiB, so below roughly 10% a difference is the machine and not the code; at 64 KiB and smaller the in-process instruments are impressions, not measurements.

nodes.label: Local Performance Baseline Suite

nodes.label: Item 2.0 Auto-Multipart Producer Measurement
nodes.rationale: The producer restructuring landed (free list of concurrency+1 buffers, workers overlapping seal and send) but the after-measurement is outstanding; until it exists no upload gain may be stated for 5.0.0.

nodes.label: Item 2.1 Stream The Client-Driven UploadPart
nodes.rationale: ReadBody materialises the whole part before the uploadId/partNumber checks and before the session lookup, nothing bounds one part, and the exit provider added a second consumer of the same buffered part.

nodes.label: Item 2.2 HTTP Transfer-Encoding Decoder Dead Branch
nodes.norm_label: item 2.2 http transfer-encoding decoder dead branch
nodes.rationale: RequiresChunkedDecoding tests r.Header.Get("Transfer-Encoding"), but net/http moves that header into r.TransferEncoding and deletes it before a handler runs, so the predicate can never be true server-side and net/http has already de-chunked the body.

nodes.label: Item 2.3 readAllSized Allocates Twice

nodes.label: Item 4.1 Discarded SDK Transport Defaults

nodes.label: Item 4.2 Fill The Pooled Buffer Before Writing
nodes.norm_label: item 4.2 fill the pooled buffer before writing
nodes.rationale: The segmented reader hands back at most one 64 KiB segment per Read regardless of len(p), so the 128 KiB pooled buffer is only half filled; the exit provider's pass-through body is the audit's original, worse shape, so a benchmark must cover both.

nodes.label: Item 6.4 Block And Mutex Profiles

nodes.label: Item 15 An Unknown Configuration Key Refuses The Start
nodes.norm_label: item 15 an unknown configuration key refuses the start
nodes.rationale: It is why this release can delete twelve keys without turning each one into a setting the operator believes is in force. viper.Unmarshal gets a DecoderConfigOption setting ErrorUnused; the provider block's mapstructure remain catch-all keeps working because a remain field nils the unused-key set before the ErrorUnused check. nodes.label: The Local Baseline Suite
nodes.rationale: Build tag perf, referenced by no workflow so CI cannot pick it up. Seven instruments, one record per run (run.json schema 1 plus REPORT.md), the machine recorded with the numbers, ratios derived at render time and never stored, and a wide-spread row marked as carrying no comparison value.

nodes.rationale: Registered and never observed - each had always reported zero, so a dashboard panel built on one was always empty.

nodes.label: P-3 The Two Headline HTTP Metrics Are Never Exported
nodes.norm_label: p-3 the two headline http metrics are never exported
nodes.rationale: RequestsTotal and RequestDuration live on a private registry that nothing gathers, while /metrics serves the default gatherer. The mechanism cuts both ways: labelled series are not exported, exported series are not labelled. No test catches it because the unit test gathers the private registry directly and the integration test only asserts /metrics answers 200.

nodes.label: Upload Falls Off A Cliff At The Routing Threshold
nodes.norm_label: upload falls off a cliff at the routing threshold
nodes.rationale: At and above 5 MiB the ratio drops from 72.2 to 59.3 percent and stays near 56-60, while every download row sits at 96.5 to 110.7 percent of direct. The crypto headroom is nearly worthless end to end - crypto is 3.8 to 6.1 percent of per-byte time - so the cliff points at the second write instead. Stated explicitly as a hypothesis: the self-copy was not timed in isolation.

nodes.label: The Self-Copy Is Not The Cause
nodes.norm_label: the self-copy is not the cause
nodes.rationale: The model needed the self-copy to run at 231-372 MiB/s; timed directly it runs at 4826-7485, an order of magnitude faster, costing about 5 percent of the gap. The hypothesis fitted three points and was wrong, which is what a model that has never been checked against the thing it models is worth.

nodes.label: The Proxy Is Faster Than The Backend When It Streams
nodes.norm_label: the proxy is faster than the backend when it streams
nodes.rationale: The streaming leg is at or above the direct backend while encrypting every byte and crossing loopback twice, so neither the cipher, nor the checksum, nor the second write, nor the extra hop is what the ratio pays for. 87 percent of the gap is the auto-multipart write path itself. Which of its two structural differences carries it is not established - attribute before fixing.

nodes.label: The Deficit Is Per Byte, Not Per Request
nodes.norm_label: the deficit is per byte, not per request
nodes.rationale: At 256 MiB the four backend calls amortise into nothing and the integrity pass is about 14 percent; three quarters of the gap scales with the bytes, and the only per-byte difference is that one leg forwards while it reads. The factor is worst at one part (1.96x) and settles near 1.45x from six parts up - the signature of a serialisation inside one part, not between parts.

nodes.label: Release Notes Skeleton
nodes.rationale: Grouped as stored data, configuration removed/renamed/refuses-to-start/new, metrics, logging, behaviour, deployment, performance claims, support and migration. The performance section states explicitly that no upload speed-up is claimed until the after-column exists.

nodes.label: Upload Path Decomposition
nodes.rationale: Decomposes the upload deficit, falsifies the explanation the pre-v2 findings proposed and identifies the real one. Taken on battery, so its figures are comparable only within the run.

nodes.label: The Before-Column For The Producer Restructuring
nodes.norm_label: the before-column for the producer restructuring
nodes.rationale: A decision like ADR 0024's is worth nothing without the column it will be judged against. On mains, clean tree, all twelve upload rows stable at 1.0-6.3 percent RSD, which is what makes the factors readable. The direct leg is dropped above 16 MiB because the backend refuses an aws-chunked chunk above that size.

nodes.label: Pooled Copy Buffer Benchmark And writerOnly
nodes.norm_label: pooled copy buffer benchmark and writeronly
nodes.rationale: copyWithPooledBuffer wraps dst in an unexported writerOnly so the pooled buffer is the copy path by construction rather than by accident of middleware composition. The decision rule was fixed before the run; 128 KiB pooled beat ReadFrom by 8.3 percent and allocated a third less.

nodes.label: Rejected: GET Read-Ahead Goroutine
nodes.rationale: The identical chain measured 218 MB/s on other hardware, so the chain was not the ~120 MB/s ceiling, and kernel socket buffers already overlap the legs for a continuous stream. Not worth a concurrency change on the integrity-critical path.

nodes.label: Same Machine, Same Power Source
nodes.rationale: The battery run of the same morning reproduces the shared sizes within noise - the battery made both legs slower together rather than distorting the comparison - but the mains run is the before-column because the run that follows it will be on mains too.

nodes.label: Exit Configuration Starts Without a License
nodes.norm_label: exit configuration starts without a license
nodes.rationale: license_file is absent on purpose: the startup gate looks only at the active provider, so this file runs unlicensed — point it at a token only if the active alias goes back to an encrypting provider.

nodes.label: config Is One String, Not a Map
nodes.norm_label: config is one string, not a map
nodes.rationale: It is passed verbatim into the ConfigMap as config.yaml — there is no config.logLevel and no config.targetEndpoint; values-development.yaml and values-monitoring.yaml do not render because they pass a map.

nodes.label: The Proxy Needs Three Things to Start
nodes.norm_label: the proxy needs three things to start
nodes.rationale: A helm install with chart defaults produces a pod that never becomes ready: the defaults are a template, not a working deployment. Configuration, license and the credentials the config references are all required.

nodes.label: AES KEK Provider
nodes.rationale: The master key is never used directly: both the wrapping key and the published fingerprint are derived with HKDF-SHA256 under separate labels, so the fingerprint reveals nothing about the key and a tampered or foreign wrap fails instead of yielding wrong key material.

nodes.label: Exit Provider (type exit)
nodes.rationale: The provider you select to leave the product: it needs no license because getting your data out must never depend on a licence being valid. It holds no key material, every write path stores what the client sent, and every read decides per object — so the aes provider that wrote the existing objects has to stay listed beside it.

nodes.label: Objects This Proxy Did Not Write Are Refused
nodes.norm_label: objects this proxy did not write are refused
nodes.rationale: The two refusals are 4xx deliberately: the state is permanent, and a 5xx would make a client SDK retry a read that cannot succeed and let a client file a corrupted object as a passing outage.

nodes.label: The License Is a Startup Gate
nodes.norm_label: the license is a startup gate
nodes.rationale: The gate looks at the active provider only, so an exit provider starts unlicensed while the aes provider beside it keeps unwrapping data keys — a license you no longer hold must never be the reason you cannot read your own data.

nodes.label: Multi-Provider Key Rotation
nodes.rationale: Every listed provider can decrypt, only encryption_method_alias writes; the read provider is chosen by the object's own s3ep-kek-fingerprint, so rotation is adding a key and keeping the old one listed. There is no re-encryption job — copying data through the proxy is the migration.

nodes.label: Four s3ep-* Object Metadata Keys
nodes.rationale: They describe only how the data key was wrapped, never the data: nonces live in the segments and the integrity value is the tag on each of them, where the backend cannot edit them. The prefix is the proxy's exclusive namespace in both directions.

nodes.label: Upgrading from 3.x or 4.x Breaks Reads
nodes.rationale: Objects written by an earlier release carry a different format id, so they are refused rather than handing out bytes the proxy cannot authenticate; type none is gone and is refused by name pointing at exit.

nodes.label: H-11 The Pass-Through Provider Was Not a Pass-Through — closed
nodes.norm_label: h-11 the pass-through provider was not a pass-through — closed
nodes.rationale: type none passed through only a single-request PUT; larger uploads sealed the object and stored its data key UNWRAPPED in s3ep-encrypted-dek, while the read path decided on the provider before looking at the object. Nothing is sealed under exit now, and EncryptDEK returns an error instead of a key.

nodes.label: H-6 An Object Without Metadata Is Served — closed
nodes.norm_label: h-6 an object without metadata is served — closed
nodes.rationale: Anyone able to write to the bucket could substitute an object by stripping four metadata keys. A refusal is permanent and has no repair path in the product: the object is restored from its source, and the 403 is the notification.

nodes.label: H-9 The Replaced Format's Decrypt Path — closed
nodes.norm_label: h-9 the replaced format's decrypt path — closed
nodes.rationale: An unauthenticated decrypt path existing only in dead code is the mirror of rule 2: not a vulnerability while unreachable, and one the moment somebody wires a caller — easy by accident, because the names read like the live ones. deadcode now reports zero unreachable functions where it reported 206.

nodes.label: License Expiry Stops the Proxy
nodes.rationale: The validator checks hourly and exits, so an expired license stops every read with it. The security consequence follows from not knowing about the exit provider: an operator facing a proxy that will not start and data they cannot read is the one who copies ciphertext out of the bucket and hunts for the key by hand.

nodes.label: The s3ep-* Namespace Filter Both Ways
nodes.norm_label: the s3ep-* namespace filter both ways
nodes.rationale: net/http canonicalises header names, so a client's x-amz-meta-s3ep-* arrived as S3ep-* and the case-sensitive filter never matched it; the backend then lowered one onto the other and the client value won often enough to leave objects permanently undecryptable. The prefix is validated against ^[a-z0-9-]+$ because an empty prefix served ciphertext behind a 200 and an upper-case one disabled decryption.

nodes.label: Reporting a Vulnerability
nodes.rationale: Private advisory only; the stated gap is that the repository carries no SECURITY.md and no dedicated security contact, and the advisory route has not been exercised.

nodes.label: AES TLS Example Configuration
nodes.rationale: The integration suite needs an HTTPS endpoint because aws-sdk-go-v2 only switches to STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER framing and checksum trailers over TLS; over plain HTTP that code path is unreachable, which is why BUG-001 shipped unnoticed.

nodes.label: Exit Provider Example Configuration
nodes.rationale: aws-chunked decoding has to stay on under pass-through: with it off the chunk framing is never stripped and lands in the stored object. The metadata prefix stays whatever the encrypting configuration used, because changing it hides the old objects from the read path.

nodes.label: What the Exit Provider Means for the Threat Model
nodes.norm_label: what the exit provider means for the threat model
nodes.rationale: Selecting exit moves the plaintext below the trust boundary on purpose — the operator's declared intent, not a defect. Three properties keep it from being a back door: the read path is unchanged for an encrypted object, the exit fingerprint is not a key (EncryptDEK/DecryptDEK both error, so a backend stamping it on an object gets a failed read rather than a data key of its choosing), and the s3ep-* namespace stays the proxy's. Switching back to an encrypting provider makes everything written during the exit period foreign — a one-way door.

nodes.label: KEK/DEK Envelope Architecture
nodes.rationale: The DEK layer is deliberately not pluggable: it is the segment chain, always. There is no second cipher, no configurable integrity mode and no format switch, so there is no DEK provider extension point.

nodes.label: Listing Parameter Behaviour
nodes.rationale: Owner names the client's own access key, never the proxy's backend account; no checksum element is emitted because a backend checksum describes the ciphertext; max-keys above 1000 is clamped by the proxy where MinIO does not clamp.

nodes.label: No Request Rate Limiting
nodes.rationale: Shipping none is a decision, not an omission: nothing is counted per caller and there is no setting for it, so a real limiter belongs in front of the proxy.

nodes.label: Sizes and Listings Describe the Plaintext
nodes.norm_label: sizes and listings describe the plaintext
nodes.rationale: Listings compute the plaintext size from the stored size, so a thousand keys cost a thousand divisions and no extra request. Under the exit provider the stored size is reported verbatim: inverting would under-report plain objects, and a sync client that believes the remote is shorter uploads over it, while over-reporting only costs a re-transfer.

nodes.label: Storage Format s3ep-gcm-seg-v2
nodes.rationale: Each seal's additional data binds the segment to its index and to the object key, so a segment cannot be moved, swapped, duplicated, dropped or reordered without the read failing — and an object copied to another name inside the backend is undecryptable there, which is why server-side copy is refused. The stored length is a pure function of the plaintext length, so any segment is found arithmetically with nothing about the layout stored where a backend could edit it.

nodes.label: Operations the Proxy Does Not Implement
nodes.norm_label: operations the proxy does not implement
nodes.rationale: An unrouted sub-resource used to fall through to the base operation for its HTTP method, which is how DELETE /bucket?encryption deleted the bucket; only allowlisted query parameters now reach the base verbs. Four sub-resources that answered 200 for work they did wrongly now answer 501.

nodes.label: What the Backend Learns Anyway
nodes.rationale: Key names in the clear, object sizes (a pure function of the plaintext length), timestamps and access patterns, which objects share a key, and how many parts an upload had. None of it is defended and none of it should be assumed hidden.

nodes.label: Backend Privilege Footprint
nodes.rationale: A declared interface method is a capability the credential is expected to have, so the 17 methods with no production caller were removed: an interface naming operations no code issues overstates the privilege the deployment needs. HEAD /bucket is answered by a ListObjectsV2 probe with MaxKeys=0, so HeadBucket permission is never needed.

nodes.label: No Multi-Tenancy
nodes.rationale: No bucket allowlist, no prefix scope, no per-client policy and no per-client key: every authenticated client can do everything any other can, and all share one backend credential. Tenant separation means one proxy per tenant.

nodes.label: Roles and Trust Boundaries
nodes.rationale: The single boundary that matters runs between the proxy and the backend: everything above it is operator-controlled and handles plaintext, everything below it is assumed adversarial. A second, weaker boundary between client and proxy is defended by SigV4.

nodes.label: HeadBucket Through the Proxy Answers 200 for a Missing Bucket
nodes.norm_label: headbucket through the proxy answers 200 for a missing bucket
nodes.rationale: HEAD /{bucket} is served as a listing with page size zero and the backend short-circuits that before checking the bucket exists, so the helper calls CreateBucket unconditionally instead of probing.

nodes.label: H-3 Rollback and Object Substitution Are Not Prevented
nodes.norm_label: h-3 rollback and object substitution are not prevented
nodes.rationale: Structural: an older version of the same key is a correctly sealed object the proxy wrote itself. Substitution across keys is closed by the object-key binding; substitution across time is not, and the only defence is the client's own consistency checks plus backend versioning and object lock.

nodes.label: The S3 Backend Is Hostile
nodes.rationale: The backend is treated as adversary, not merely untrusted: it can read, alter, swap, replay, truncate and lie in listings, metadata, ETags and errors. Nothing it says counts as authentication — a 200 and a TLS leg are statements about availability and the network, not about integrity of the stored object.

nodes.label: Handlers That Refuse Rather Than Pretend
nodes.norm_label: handlers that refuse rather than pretend
nodes.rationale: An operation that answers 200 for work it did not do is worse than one that refuses — the legal-hold handler always set the hold ON, ?attributes returned object bytes where an XML document was expected, and UploadPartCopy was unreachable and stored an empty part.

nodes.label: The Three Rules
nodes.rationale: 1) Integrity means the proxy verifies. 2) A control that exists only in configuration or documentation is worse than no control, because it gets relied upon. 3) The stored-object format may change without a migration path.

nodes.rationale: hex(SHA-256(key)) turned the published fingerprint into an offline verification oracle for a low-entropy or published key. Closed by deriving under its own label and by refusing a key that is not base64 of 32 bytes, printable-only, or under 16 distinct byte values. What remains and is accepted: the fingerprint links deployments that share a master key.

nodes.norm_label: the chart does not roll pods on a config change
nodes.rationale: No checksum/config annotation, so helm upgrade reports success while old pods keep the old key encrypting every new object — the deployment tooling hands the operator a false statement about the security of their data. Rule 2, precisely.

nodes.label: KEK Fingerprint by HKDF Label
nodes.rationale: Fingerprints are derived, not configured, so they cannot drift; derived under a label of its own, publishing it in object metadata says nothing about the key. The exit fingerprint is a constant no object ever carries, so meeting it in metadata means the backend put it there.

nodes.label: KEK Rotation by Fingerprint
nodes.rationale: Rotation is the one thing the metadata design is built for: add the provider, repoint the alias, restart. There is no RotateKEK call — the KeyEncryptor interface is EncryptDEK, DecryptDEK, Name, Fingerprint and nothing else.

nodes.label: Two-Layer Key Hierarchy
nodes.rationale: There is no third key layer: integrity is not a value derived alongside the data and stored next to it, it is the tag on every segment produced by the same operation that encrypts it. A fresh DEK per object from crypto/rand, never reused, and no nonce reused under one DEK.

nodes.label: Associated Data: formatID, Object Key, Index
nodes.norm_label: associated data: formatid, object key, index
nodes.rationale: Binding the client's object key stops a hostile backend serving object A's ciphertext under B's name - it can copy the metadata too, so metadata alone binds nothing. The bucket is deliberately out, so a ciphertext bucket can be replicated wholesale without re-encryption; the residual is a cross-bucket same-key swap and rollback, which no AEAD prevents.

nodes.label: Four Encryption Metadata Keys
nodes.rationale: encrypted-dek, dek-algorithm, kek-algorithm, kek-fingerprint - all four known at PutObject and CreateMultipartUpload time because EncryptDEK takes only the DEK and the object key, never the ciphertext. That is what removes the self-CopyObject. aes-iv and hmac are gone.

nodes.label: Item 2d Sealed Checksum Read Side And Tail-First Read
nodes.norm_label: item 2d sealed checksum read side and tail-first read
nodes.rationale: HEAD becomes one GetObject with Range bytes=-40 so it reports the authenticated plaintext length; a whole-object GET requests bytes=-65604 first, then the remainder with If-Match. Ranged reads carry no checksum because aws-sdk-go-v2 validates response checksums only on status 200, never on a 206.

nodes.label: Sealed Trailer With Length And CRC32C
nodes.norm_label: sealed trailer with length and crc32c
nodes.rationale: CRC32C measured 12.1 GB/s against SHA-256 3.4 and CRC-64 2.4; SHA-256 also lost on not being combinable across out-of-order or re-uploaded parts. The checksum lives sealed in the trailer rather than in metadata because a plaintext checksum in cleartext metadata hands a hostile backend a confirmation oracle for low-entropy objects.

nodes.label: Segmented AES-256-GCM Chain Format
nodes.rationale: One object is a chain of 64 KiB segments (nonce 12 + GCM + tag 16) closed by a 40-byte trailer, all under one per-object DEK. S is a constant of the format, not a configuration value: 28 B per 64 KiB is 0.043 percent overhead, the knee where per-segment cost is negligible and the working set still fits in cache.

nodes.label: Plaintext Size As A Pure Function Of Stored Size
nodes.norm_label: plaintext size as a pure function of stored size
nodes.rationale: n = ceil((C-40)/(S+28)), P = C-40-28n. Lets HEAD, GET and LIST report the plaintext length with no per-object round trip. It is not redundant with the trailer: the function converts a length the backend reports, and the backend is the adversary; the trailer is the authenticated copy.

nodes.label: The Segment Codec, Measured
nodes.rationale: The prediction was 3.4x from a model of raw cipher calls; the shipped codec measures 1.74-1.87x. The gap is the CRC32C the model did not run, plus segment framing and the trailer. The model rows stay in the suite as a ceiling, not a target: the checksum is decided.

nodes.label: Random Inline Nonces Per Segment
nodes.rationale: S3 multipart has no single sequential writer: a part can be uploaded again with different content, so a derived nonce would be reused with a different plaintext, costing confidentiality of both plaintexts and the authentication key. A random 96-bit nonce removes the case for 12 bytes per 64 KiB; the SP 800-38D bound is far away because the DEK is per object.

nodes.label: Rejected: AES-CTR Plus Per-Segment HMAC
nodes.rationale: Reaches the same property and pays more: two primitives, the slower doing the integrity work, two passes where AES-GCM is one, identical layout work, and none of the deletions become possible. Same cost, no simplification.

nodes.label: Rejected: Storing A Per-Object Part Layout
nodes.norm_label: rejected: storing a per-object part layout
nodes.rationale: If client parts may have any size the segment-to-offset mapping must be stored somewhere; every place considered was worse than constraining part sizes and doing the arithmetic.

nodes.label: Rejected: Tink AES-GCM-HKDF Derived Nonces
nodes.rationale: Tink's streaming construction assumes a single sequential writer, which S3 multipart is not - it is N-3 in a new costume.

nodes.label: Rejected: XChaCha20-Poly1305
nodes.rationale: Random-nonce-safe by design but 2 to 4 times slower than hardware AES-GCM at this segment size, for a margin that is already sufficient.

nodes.label: A 1.7x That Was Nearly A 1.0x
nodes.rationale: Two implementation choices cost the entire gain: folding the CRC per 64 KiB segment with the GF(2) matrix construction (4523 against 12107 MB/s for a running checksum - the fold belongs at part granularity), and copying every byte into the writer's pending buffer even when the caller handed over a whole segment. The lesson: an instrument comparing a model against a real path measures the model.

nodes.label: Item 4.3 GOMEMLIMIT
nodes.rationale: GOGC stays default and GOGC=off is excluded while any client-controlled full-body allocation exists. The GOMAXPROCS/automaxprocs half is void: since Go 1.25 the Linux runtime derives GOMAXPROCS from the cgroup CPU limit.

nodes.label: Item 6.1 Baseline Without Backend TLS
nodes.rationale: About 10-16 percent of proxy CPU in every recorded profile is TLS re-encryption towards a loopback MinIO with insecure_skip_verify - zero endpoint-authentication value, and it is misread as object crypto.

nodes.label: Item 6.3 Small-Object Request-Rate Ceiling
nodes.rationale: The proxy does not get faster when the client asks for more at once (1778/2357/1930 ops/s at c1/c8/c32) while the backend scales 2.6x. Identical on TLS, so it is per-request serialisation, not a transport or throughput limit.

nodes.norm_label: p-11 plain-http backend cannot take a streaming upload
nodes.rationale: aws-sdk-go-v2 signs by hashing the body, which needs a seekable stream, and only accepts UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD over TLS.

nodes.label: The HMAC Is The Entire Difference
nodes.norm_label: the hmac is the entire difference
nodes.rationale: HMAC-SHA256 runs at 3092 MiB/s against AES-CTR at 10475, so the large-object path can never exceed the HMAC however fast the cipher is. In the proxy's own profile SHA-256 is 17.30 percent flat against AES-CTR 5.17 - the integrity pass is 3.3x the cipher it protects.

nodes.label: The Container Memory Limit Is Nowhere Near Reached
nodes.norm_label: the container memory limit is nowhere near reached
nodes.rationale: Settled idle 97.7 MiB, peak under load 124.1, container limit 512. A GOMEMLIMIT at about 400 MiB is never approached, so the collector has no reason to behave differently and there is no mechanism for a 3-5 percent gain; the honest outcome may be to ship it as an out-of-memory guard and claim no throughput benefit.

nodes.label: Ranged Reads: The Alignment Before-Column
nodes.rationale: A deliberately unaligned offset is indistinguishable from an aligned one at 1 MiB and above because AES-CTR seeks to any byte. A segment chain cannot, so these numbers are the only before-column for the row to watch after the format change - measured before the code that will make them interesting existed.

nodes.label: The Proxy Barely Gets Faster With More Clients
nodes.norm_label: the proxy barely gets faster with more clients
nodes.rationale: The backend scales 2.8x from one client to eight while the proxy gains 1.3x and gives it back at 32. Identical on both transports, so not a transport effect; at 64 KiB the proxy runs far below the crypto floor, so not bandwidth. Where the serialisation lives is not established - the CPU profile was taken under large-object load.

nodes.label: RSA Unwrap Is Four Orders Of Magnitude Off The Local Provider
nodes.norm_label: rsa unwrap is four orders of magnitude off the local provider
nodes.rationale: AES-256 unwrap 146 ns against RSA-4096 3.80 ms - 26000x. The wrap column is far closer because wrapping uses the public exponent; it is the read path that pays. This is the measurement behind keeping one local key provider.

nodes.label: pre-v2 Baseline Findings
nodes.rationale: The before column for the storage format change. Written the day the numbers were taken, stating what they support, what they only suggest, and what they cannot answer; derived and single-sample figures are marked as such.

nodes.label: The GCM Profile Rows Are TLS Records, Not Object Crypto
nodes.norm_label: the gcm profile rows are tls records, not object crypto
nodes.rationale: pprof -peek reaches gcmAesEnc/Dec only through crypto/tls xorNonceAEAD: they are the proxy-to-backend hop. Counting them as object crypto is exactly the misattribution this project has already made once and that the measurement rules were written to prevent.

nodes.label: Two Measurement Bugs Found Before The Run
nodes.norm_label: two measurement bugs found before the run
nodes.rationale: One variant allocated a destination per repetition while the other reused one, and the segmented decrypt allocated per segment - two thousand allocations for a 128 MiB object. A comparison between two crypto paths is only valid if both allocate the same amount, which for a throughput number means both allocating nothing.

nodes.label: Published Checksum Cost Table
nodes.rationale: Apple M5 Pro, one core, 64 KiB blocks, Go 1.27: CRC32 and CRC32C 12 GB/s, AES-GCM seal 9.1, SHA-1 3.5, SHA-256 3.4, MD5 0.95. MD5 costs about ten times the encryption pass per byte and lands on kopia's uploads. The switch that would have traded this away was withdrawn before it was built; the measurement survives as a published table, not a gate.

nodes.label: CRC64NVME Slicing-By-8 Rebuild Trap
nodes.rationale: crc64.MakeTable caches only ISO and ECMA; for any other polynomial crc64.update rebuilds a 16 KiB slicing-by-8 table on every Write of 2048 bytes or more. Build the table once into a package-level var and run the update loop directly.

nodes.label: DeleteObjects Requires And Verifies A Digest
nodes.norm_label: deleteobjects requires and verifies a digest
nodes.rationale: The cost argument that produced the withdrawn switch was about multi-megabyte uploads, not a delete document of a few kilobytes.

nodes.label: aws-chunked Trailer Capture
nodes.rationale: bufio.ReadString returns data together with io.EOF when the last line has no terminator, so the capture must parse the partial line first. A trailer named in X-Amz-Trailer that never arrives is a failed verification, not a missing one - otherwise omitting it is a free opt-out.

nodes.label: verifyingReader
nodes.rationale: Hashes the decoded payload as it passes and compares at EOF, wrapped around whichever reader Parser.ReadBody or Parser.StreamingReader returns, so there is one pass and no extra copy. The handler must ask the verifier directly rather than errors.Is through net/http, url.Error and smithy wrapping.

nodes.label: The Unprotected Client-To-Proxy Leg
nodes.rationale: A byte corrupted before the proxy encrypts is encrypted faithfully and authenticated faithfully, so every integrity mechanism the product has confirms the corruption. The upload checksum is the only check that can catch it, and it is the only one the proxy runs on that leg.

nodes.label: Never Forwarded, Never Stored, Never Echoed
nodes.norm_label: never forwarded, never stored, never echoed
nodes.rationale: A plaintext checksum written in cleartext metadata next to the ciphertext hands a hostile backend a confirmation oracle for a small or low-entropy object. Echoing is pointless: no SDK examined reads the PutObject response checksum, and the value is the client's own number anyway.
